name.text: MQH - Evaluating the Convergence and Value of the Improper Integral_Research

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the integral below and determine if it converges or diverges.

Note: \( \infty\) is entered as inf and \( -\infty\) is entered as minf.

\(\displaystyle \int_{{@lower_lm@}}^{{@upper_lm@}}{@fx@}\,dx=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

Therefore, the integral is [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution

Recall that we can’t evaluate the integral as long as there is an infinity in one of the limits. Therefore, we’ll need to replace infinity with a parameter \(t\) as follows,

The given improper integral is

\(\displaystyle I = \int_{@lower_lm@}^{{@upper_lm@}}{@fx@} \, dx. \)

We will first evaluate whether the integral converges or diverges by finding the limit of the integral as \( t \to \infty \):

\( \displaystyle I = \int_{@lower_lm@}^{{@t@}}{@fx@} \, dx. \)

The antiderivative of \(\displaystyle {@fx@} \) is:

\(\displaystyle \int {@fx@} \, dx = {@indef_int@} \)

Now, evaluate the integral from \( {@lower_lm@} \) to \( t\):

\(\displaystyle I(t) = \left[ {@indef_int@} \right]_ {@lower_lm@}^t = {@indef_val@}\)

Take the limit as \( t \to \infty \)

\(\displaystyle I = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left( {@indef_val@}\right) = {@def_integral@} \)

The improper integral is {@mcq_correct(ta_4)[1]@}, and its exact value is \( \boxed{{@def_integral@}} \).

hint.text:
This is an improper integral because the upper limit is \(\infty \). So, you need to rewrite the integral in terms of a limit:

\(\displaystyle \int_{{@lower_lm@}}^{{@upper_lm@}}{@fx@}\,dx=\lim_{b \to \infty } \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_lm@}}^{{@upper_lm@}}{@fx@}\,dx\)

Solve the integral taking the upper limit as finite.

The integrand, \(\displaystyle {@fx@}\,dx\) is a rational function of \(x\), which suggests a standard power rule for integration.

\(\displaystyle \int\frac{1}{(x+a)^n}\,dx=\displaystyle \frac{(x+a)^{(1-n)}}{1-n}\) for \(n\neq 1\)

Start by recognizing that the integrand is a rational function with the form \(\displaystyle \frac{{@num@}}{({@(x+denom_const)@})^p} \), where \(\displaystyle p ={@power@} \).

Recall that for Integrals of the form \( \int \frac{1}{(x+c)^p} \, dx \), the antiderivative is:

\(\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{(x+c)^p} \, dx = \frac{(x+c)^{1-p}}{1-p} + C \)

Here, the exponent is \( p ={@power@} \), so the antiderivative can be computed by applying this formula.
